strengths: Novel canonical orientation normalization technique that elegantly solves the arbitrary pose problem in class-pose decomposition with strong theoretical justification via Proposition 3.1
Strong theoretical foundation with rigorous mathematical grounding in group theory and Fréchet means, including formal proofs of convergence in Wasserstein distance
Comprehensive experimental validation on both synthetic (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST) and real-world data (molecular conformations), successfully recovering complex symmetries including SO(2) and SO(3)
Clear demonstration of interpretability advantages over existing methods, with data-aligned canonical poses (e.g., upright digits) versus arbitrary orientations
Practical applications demonstrated (OOD pose detection with AUC 0.92-0.80, molecular conformation analysis) showing real-world relevance beyond toy problems
Excellent reproducibility with publicly available code, detailed implementation details in appendices, and comprehensive experimental setup descriptions
Ability to handle challenging cases including partial symmetries (e.g., distinguishing 6's from 9's related by 180° but not full SO(2) equivalence)
weaknesses: Limited scope of demonstrated symmetries restricted primarily to rotation groups (SO(2), SO(3)); framework claims generality to arbitrary Lie groups but lacks validation on reflection symmetries or discrete groups
Incomplete experimental comparisons with only SGM and IE-AE as direct baselines; missing quantitative comparisons with other recent symmetry discovery methods mentioned in related work
Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: choice of k=25 neighbors appears arbitrary with no systematic method provided, and only limited sensitivity analysis shown
MNIST/Fashion-MNIST evaluation uses artificially labeled data with known ground-truth symmetries, validating recovery but not fully testing discovery from truly unknown distributions
Molecular conformations evaluation focuses on reconstruction quality rather than validating discovered symmetries, lacking quantitative ground truth and comparison with structure-based methods
Insufficient failure analysis: no systematic discussion of failure cases, robustness to noise/corruption, computational complexity limitations, or edge cases with complex partial symmetries

Presentation clarity issues: dense mathematical notation could be simplified, connection between canonical orientation normalization and symmetric discovery could be more intuitive, some key details relegated to appendix
Limited statistical rigor: some results lack error bars or significance testing, single runs shown without confidence intervals, and limited discussion of variance across different initializations

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying concrete limitation (arbitrary canonicals in class-pose methods) with well-motivated solution
Solid theoretical contribution with Proposition 3.1 providing convergence guarantees in Wasserstein distance and rigorous proofs
Comprehensive experimental validation spanning 2D (MNIST, FashionMNIST) and 3D (GEOM-QM9) with first SO(3) symmetry discovery demonstrations
Practical value: architecture-agnostic test-time canonicalization without retraining shows significant improvements (92.94% vs 66.90% on Rot-MNIST)
Thoughtful handling of multimodal distributions via Tukey-Fréchet mean extension with clear motivation and convergence analysis
Ability to distinguish classes related by group transformations (digits 6 and 9), which full equivariance methods cannot achieve
Extensive ablation studies, implementation details, and reproducibility artifacts (promised code release, hyperparameter documentation)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution (right-multiplication by inverse Fréchet mean) uses standard statistical tools (Fréchet means, M-estimators) without significant methodological innovation
Fundamental dependence on class-pose decomposition methods (IE-AEs), which are niche architectures, limiting practical applicability and scope of impact
Equivalence class definition via k-NN proximity in invariant space Z is heuristic and lacks theoretical justification; assumes well-separated clusters that may not exist
Weak baseline comparisons: SGM (closest related work) compared only qualitatively; missing quantitative symmetry recovery accuracy comparisons
Limited real-world evaluation: image experiments only on synthetic rotations of MNIST/FashionMNIST; no natural image experiments where acknowledged background/object context challenges arise
Approximately 20% of molecules show high prediction error (MSE > 800) on GEOM-QM9 (Figure 5d); root causes not identified beyond ruling out molecular size/flexibility correlation
Theoretical assumptions restrictive: assumes s = ρ_X(g)γ[x] + ε_s with ||ε_s|| < ε' (small noise) and well-defined classes; realistic validity on diverse data unclear
No computational complexity analysis; scalability of k-NN searches and Fréchet mean computations to large-scale datasets not discussed
